person.name: Ghifari Nafhan
person.headline: I build AI that turns hours of manual work into minutes.
person.description: Software engineer automating slow, manual work with AI, end to end from data to UI. Case studies, build logs and production AI lessons.
person.about: Most of his work sits between backend systems, data and turning an idea into something people use every day. Lately that means LLM features: assistants grounded in real data, agents that call tools instead of guessing, evals that catch regressions, and the pipelines and UI around them. He has shipped across healthtech, education, finance and internal tools. He cares about deterministic code for anything touching money or records, and a human approval step where mistakes are expensive. He is finishing an applied bachelor's in Software Engineering Technology at Universitas Gadjah Mada, where he was a practicum assistant and coordinator for two years.

work.title: CatatAja
work.summary: A personal finance assistant on WhatsApp. Type, snap a receipt or send a voice note; an LLM understands it and a deterministic ledger records it.
work.text: The problem Most people stop tracking their money for a boring reason: typing every expense into an app is tedious. Chat is different. Sending "lunch 25k" to a contact you already have open takes two seconds. So the idea was simple. Let people record expenses and income in WhatsApp, by text, receipt photo or voice note, and give them a web dashboard for the bigger picture. The hard part is that a language model is a bad bookkeeper. It is great at reading "bought coffee and bread, 40k total" and very good at sounding sure. It is not something you want computing a balance. What I built CatatAja is a WhatsApp-first backend in FastAPI with LangGraph orchestration, plus a React dashboard. The agent's job is understanding: what did the person mean, which tool should run, how should the reply read. Everything that touches money lives in plain service code: ledger writes, balances, plan limits, idempotency. Gemini handles receipt photos and voice notes directly, so the first version didn't need a separate OCR or speech service, or a heavy task queue. The dashboard adds budgets, custom categories, an Excel export with live formulas, and login through a one-time link sent over WhatsApp, so nobody needs a password. Decisions that mattered 1. Don't let the model do the money math. The model routes and summarizes. Service code writes the ledger and computes every total. A wrong category is annoying; a wrong balance means nobody trusts the app again. Keeping arithmetic out of the model made the dangerous failures impossible instead of just unlikely. 2. work.title: Inbox assistant: every request on one board
work.summary: A read-only AI assistant that collects work requests from my chat apps, proposes tickets for my tracker, and drafts my standups. I approve everything.
work.text: The problem If you work with more than one team, your to-do list doesn't live in one place. It lives in whatever app someone used to message you. Mine was split everywhere. A campus assignment in one app, a request from a lecturer in another, a teammate in a third. On top of that, one of my teams runs a daily standup, so every evening I had to answer one question: what did I actually get done today? Some things I fixed in minutes and forgot. Some only existed as one line in a chat I scrolled past. Keeping track of my work had quietly become a second job, and all of it was manual: remember, write it down, remember again at standup time. I kept thinking: "why am I the one doing the remembering?" What I built I spent about a week building an assistant that does the remembering for me. It reads my chats and tells me what people asked for, turns those requests into tickets once I approve them, checks at the end of the day for work that never got a ticket, and drafts my daily standup. The setup is plain: - It's a Plan , a self-hosted issue tracker on my own server. It ships an MCP server, so an AI client can read and update issues. - My chat apps , connected read-only: MCP servers where they exist, and a gateway on my own server, reachable only from inside it, where they don't. - Claude Code as the client that does the reading, matching and drafting. Everything goes into one tracker project, with one label per area of my life. I considered separate projects, but I want one board that answers "what do I do next?", not five. work.title: Outbreak investigation platform
work.summary: A full-stack platform for field investigations: questionnaires with conditional logic, anonymous public submissions with location, and per-organization quotas.
work.text: The problem When an outbreak is being investigated, the questions you need to ask depend on the answers you just got. "Are you sick?" If yes, ask about symptoms and when they started. If no, skip all of that. A static form either asks irrelevant questions or misses the ones that matter. There's a second problem. Some of the data has to come from people who will never create an account: residents or respondents reached through a shared link. They need to submit quickly, anonymously, and ideally with a location attached. And because several organizations share the platform, each one needs limits on projects, submissions and team members that the system actually enforces. What I built A NestJS and TypeORM backend on PostgreSQL, with a Next.js frontend using TanStack Query. Organizations create projects, build questionnaires, invite project managers and investigators, and collect responses either through the authenticated app or through public links. The core pieces: - A questionnaire builder with conditional logic. Each field can carry rules like show if, hide if, require if, enable if and disable if, pointing at another question's answer. - Public sharing. A questionnaire can be shared through a token link. Anyone with the link can submit without an account, with optional GPS capture and reverse geocoding. - Quotas and roles. Organizations have limits on projects, submissions and members, with voucher redemption and an audit trail. Invitations check and reserve quota before they're sent. - A typed API contract. work.title: NutriPlate
work.summary: An AI nutrition tracker: photograph a meal, get a nutrition estimate, and follow calories and weight in an installable web app.
work.text: The problem Tracking what you eat works, but almost nobody keeps doing it. Logging a meal by hand means finding each ingredient, guessing portions, and typing it all in, three times a day. NutriPlate tries to remove that step. You take a photo of your plate, the app estimates the nutrition, and the meal goes into your log. Around that sit calorie and weight tracking, an onboarding flow that sets your targets, and a nutrition chatbot. I co-founded NutriPlate and led the engineering. The interesting part, looking back, is less any single feature and more how the system had to change shape as it grew. What I built The first version ran on Next.js and Firebase. Later I redesigned it around a Go backend. That rebuild grew out of NutriSmart, our entry for the GEMASTIK national competition: a Next.js PWA in front, a Go REST API on PostgreSQL behind it, Midtrans for payments, everything in Docker. That version added AI meal scanning, calorie and weight dashboards, and a multi-agent nutrition chatbot. In 2026 I consolidated the backend, the admin panel and the consumer app into one monorepo. That version brought a redesigned eight-step onboarding with a BMR calculator, AI scanning through Genkit and the OpenAI API with schema validation on the results, and an admin side for monitoring scan activity and auditing meal history. Decisions that mattered 1. Move from Firebase to a Go backend. Once there were subscriptions, payments and gated features, the logic needed a home of its own. The Go API on PostgreSQL owns meals, recipes, body metrics, subscriptions and payment webhooks.…

work.title: From 3 hours to 3 minutes: a lab report grading agent
work.summary: Two AI agents that turn weekly lab report grading into a short review: one writes the grading guide, one grades against it, and I make the final call.
work.text: The problem As a practicum teaching assistant at Universitas Gadjah Mada, I spent nearly 3 hours every week grading lab reports. The work matters. Students learn from the feedback, and the grade has to be fair. But it was also very repetitive. For every report I checked the same things: does it cover the theory, is the methodology right, do the conclusions follow, is the formatting correct. Week after week, the same process with different content. I kept thinking: "if it's repetitive and follows a pattern, it can probably be automated." The catch is that grading is a judgment call. I didn't want a system that hands out grades on its own. I wanted one that does the tedious reading and checking, and leaves the decision to me. What I built A grading pipeline with two agents, each with one job. First, the Guide Maker Agent . It builds the grading guide: the rubric that says what a good report for this assignment should contain, across theory, methodology, conclusions and formatting. Second, the Grading Agent . It reads each student report and grades it against that guide. Then I review. I go through the agent's assessment and make the final decision on every grade. Decisions that mattered 1. Write the guide before grading anything. Splitting the work into a guide maker and a grader means every report is measured against the same written standard, not against whatever the model happens to focus on in that report. 2. One agent, one job. Making a rubric and applying a rubric are different tasks. Keeping them in separate agents keeps each one's instructions short and its output…

work.title: RT 06 Citran community portal
work.summary: A heritage and news portal for a Kotagede neighborhood, with a CMS that lets non-technical admins edit text directly on the live page.
work.text: The problem RT 06 Citran is a neighborhood in the Kotagede heritage corridor, in Bantul, Yogyakarta. I built its web portal during KKN, Universitas Gadjah Mada's community service program, where students live in and work with a local community. The neighborhood wanted a place to show its heritage sites, publish local news, and share its community rules. That part is a normal website. The real constraint was what happens after we leave. The people who would keep the site up to date are neighborhood officers, not developers. They needed to keep news and announcements current without learning a technical CMS dashboard, with its content types, fields and separate preview. What I built An editorial portal in Next.js with a custom design language drawn from Javanese batik: a sogan and turmeric palette and a hand-built SVG Kawung pattern. It has pages for heritage sites, community activity reports, a history timeline, the neighborhood regulations (the original poster next to a full-text transcription), and the board of officers. Behind it sits a small CMS on Supabase: - Inline editing. A signed-in officer sees the public page as usual, plus a floating toolbar. They click a piece of text, edit it in place, and save. No dashboard. - Admin pages for activity reports and board members, with photo uploads straight from a phone camera into storage. - An org chart that builds itself from the position titles officers type in.
